overview: A difficult, multi-pitch technical alpine rock climb up Mount Persis's sheer north face, established by prolific North Cascades first-ascentionist Bryan Burdo.
beta: Known only as a difficult alpine rock climb by Bryan Burdo on Persis's north face — no detailed grade, pitch count, or topo is available. This is a serious, low-traffic line distinct from the peak's Class 2 West Ridge hiking route; treat it as an alpine rock objective requiring full trad rack, rope, and North Cascades route-finding/approach skills rather than a hiking route.

first_pass.evidence: Only described as a 'difficult Bryan Burdo alpine rock climb' on the north face; no published grade found.
first_pass.note: The record has no grade either; leave ungraded.

overview: An off-trail scramble alternative to the standard trail, climbing from Pinnacle Lake through Iodine Gulch to the scenic Bathtub Lakes basin on Mount Pilchuck's east side, with the option to continue west across talus to the summit lookout.
beta: A documented Mountaineers alpine-scramble route (10 miles round trip, 2,800 ft gain) that leaves the maintained trail network at Pinnacle Lake. There is no maintained trail beyond the lake, so the route involves genuine off-trail navigation, bushwhacking, and rock scrambling through two steep sections before reaching the Bathtub Lakes basin. Many parties treat Bathtub Lakes as the objective and turn around there; others continue scrambling west to join Mount Pilchuck's summit boulder field and l

first_pass.evidence: Mountaineers: to Bathtub Lakes Technical 2; on to the summit Technical 3 (steep gully and talus).

ice_grade: Steep alpine ice (unrated by FA party)
fa: Dee Molenaar and Bob Craig, July 15, 1948
overview: A direct line threading the steep, broken ice of the Nisqually Glacier icefall on the south side. An engaging steep-ice and serac-navigation objective that demands cold conditions and speed through threatened terrain.
beta: First climbed July 15, 1948 after roughly ten hours of intensive ice work through jumbled seracs and crevasses, including a knife-edge section requiring step-chopping, before reaching Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft.
breakdown: Upper icefall to Wapowety Cleaver: Ice blocks, knife-edge
Upper Nisqually Glacier to Kautz route: Glacier, crevassed

first_pass.evidence: First climbed 1948 (Molenaar, Craig); route listings give Alpine Grade III with ice to ~60 degrees; no published AI grade.
first_pass.note: No ice grade exists; 60-degree serac ice mapped to AI3 as a best reading.

face: North face, between Liberty Ridge and Curtis Ridge
fa: Charles Bell, solo, via the West Rib, June 1961
overview: A notorious ~3,600-foot north face — the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's cirque — capped by a 200-300 ft band of hanging ice (seracs) that has historically deterred most attempts and is the wall's defining objective hazard. Named for geological engineer Bailey Willis, who helped build the first trail to the Carbon Glacier in 1881. The wall's West Rib was first climbed in June 1961 by Charles ('Charlie') Bell, though credit for the first ascent was disputed for years; Jim Wickwire (who climbed t
beta: Mixed alpine terrain requiring pins, screws, nuts, and cams; multiple lines/linkups exist (e.g., the East Rib, and 'Traverse of the Angels' style link-ups), but the wall as a whole is rarely climbed given the objective danger.
breakdown: Bergschrund and lower ribs: Snow, 45°, rock bands
Upper wall and ice cliff: Mixed, 50–60° ice

first_pass.evidence: MP grades the wall M5+ X, Grade V (a mixed grade); other sources say it is not technically hard by modern standards and the danger is the 300 ft serac band.
first_pass.note: MP's only grade is mixed (M5+ X), which none of the three scales can hold; AI3 kept from the record's ice_grade as a best reading. Several ribs exist (East Rib, Central Rib, Brumal Buttress) and the record does not say which one.

face: North side of Nooksack Ridge, above Ruth Creek
overview: A confined snow/ice/rock couloir on Sefrit's north side (also called the North Couloir), climbing about 1,800 feet from talus above Ruth Creek to gain the upper snow slopes of Nooksack Ridge near the summit crest.
beta: From the trail along Ruth Creek at about 3,450 ft, drop southwest across the creek and cross talus to the base of the couloir at roughly 4,000 ft. The couloir is a confined, box-canyon-like chute — its name reflects obvious snow, ice, and rockfall danger — and is climbed for about 1,800 vertical feet to reach the upper snow slopes of Nooksack Ridge, from which Sefrit's high point is gained by further ridge travel. A helmet is considered essential given the objective hazard in the chute.

first_pass.evidence: SummitPost: ~1,800 ft confined couloir to Nooksack Ridge, a basic snow climb with some 3rd-4th class rock at the end.
first_pass.note: The couloir itself is snow (sometimes ice); the 3rd-4th class finish sets the grade.

overview: The NE Ridge of the summit pyramid is a harder, seldom-done technical finish (up to 5.7) used as an alternative to the standard pyramid gully by parties topping out from the North Face, Hanging Glacier, or NW Rib lines on Shuksan's north side.
beta: Moderate rock climbing between 4th class and 5.7 gains the exposed summit block; it requires additional ice climbing lower down to reach the base of the ridge and complex alpine rock-finding higher up. It is generally regarded as an alternate finish rather than a fully independent line from base to summit.

first_pass.evidence: Guide service lists the Northeast Ridge among the north-side summit pyramid finishes, which 'all involve moderate rock climbing between 4th Class and 5.6'.
first_pass.note: No source found for the record's 5.7; only this collective 4th-5.6 statement.

fa: Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney, 1942 (peak/route first ascent, part of the brothers' 1942 Washington Pass tower campaign)
overview: Mushroom Tower is a slender granite tower at the north end of Kangaroo Ridge, immediately north of Big Kangaroo (8,280 ft), above Washington Pass on the North Cascades Highway (SR 20). It takes its name from a blocky, overhanging summit block that must be gained via a short, exposed step-across — a memorable finish to an otherwise moderate low-5th-class scramble/climb.
beta: From the base of the tower, a single pitch of mid-5th-class (roughly 5.5) climbing leads directly to Mushroom Tower's small, exposed, lopsided summit block. It is commonly combined with nearby Big Kangaroo and/or Melted Tower, which share the same Kangaroo Ridge approach, for a bigger day out.

first_pass.evidence: Trip reports: one pitch of mid fifth-class to the summit, rap off two old 1/4in bolts; no route page gives a number
first_pass.note: Record itself splits 5.4 (grade) vs 5.5 (rock_grade); took the top, consistent with 'mid fifth'

rock_grade: 3rd class (one short step, on Kindy Ridge below Snowking's summit)
alpine_grade: Mountaineers Scramble S4 / Terrain T5 (rated for the Snowking Mtn NE Shoulder portion that this route climbs first)
face: Mutchler Glacier cirque, on Snowking Mountain's southeast ridge
overview: Mutchler Peak (7,150 ft; referenced in some older trip reports as 'Snowqueen') is a remote summit in the Buckindy Group of the Cascade River backcountry, part of the rugged, semi-glaciated ridge system southeast of Marblemount that also includes Snowking Mountain (7,433'), Mount Buckindy (7,320'), Mount Misch (7,435'), Bruseth Mountain (7,220'), and Mount Chaval to the east. There is no maintained trail to Mutchler; it sits in roadless country between the Cascade River and Suiattle River drainag
beta: Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Parties reach it either by continuing the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past the summit and along the connecting ridge/snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or from the south on the longer Green Mountain–Mount Misch–Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mut

first_pass.evidence: Traverse reports: heather ramp on Mutchler's NE ridge to the flat summit plateau on easy ground; Class 3 ramp/steps on the glacier approach
first_pass.note: Glacier can have a short blue-ice section late season

rock_grade: Class 3 (talus scramble on the upper north ridge once snow-free)
ice_grade: Can be firm/icy snow requiring crampons and an ice axe (on one May ascent it was startlingly icy and smooth, demanding committing crampon work)
overview: An alternative, more direct line up North Gardner's north side: a trail-less approach past a ford of Cedar Creek leads to a broad northwest-facing snow couloir that climbs directly toward the summit, finishing with a stretch of loose talus along the upper north ridge.
beta: From the Cedar Creek Trail, parties leave the trail to bushwhack toward Cedar Creek, ford it (difficulty varies greatly with flow — see Watch Out), and continue cross-country along/above the Shelokum Creek drainage to open terrain below a broad, moderately angled northwest couloir. The couloir has been climbed on foot (crampons) and descended on skis; above the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of dry, loose talus on the north ridge leads to the summit. A 2024 ascent found the snow "shockingly
breakdown: Northwest couloir (snow): Moderate snow slope, can firm to hard ice

first_pass.evidence: Cedar Creek/NW couloir reports describe a straightforward snow climb, then Class 3 talus on the upper north ridge; snow can be firm or icy
first_pass.note: Moderate snow couloir (crampons when firm) mapped to its Class 3 rock finish

fa: Lionel Chute and Victor Kaartinen, July 1929 (disputed)
overview: Alpine rock climbing on the northeast-facing aspect of Mount Index, featuring Class 4-5 scrambling and mixed rock pitches on primarily solid granite.
beta: This route is less frequently documented than other Index routes. The northeast face offers an intermediate alpine rock objective with mixed scrambling and roped pitches. Route quality and exact character are variable; climbing conditions greatly affect difficulty.

first_pass.evidence: No route-specific source found for a Northeast Buttress on Index's North Peak; value read from the record's own columns

rock_grade: Class 3-4 scramble (crux ~100 ft summit step, locally graded 3.5)
face: South/east flank (opposite the mountain's west-side ridge)
overview: North Star Mountain sits immediately west of Bonanza Peak in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, above the Railroad Creek and Lyman Lakes basins. No maintained trail reaches the summit; the standard route climbs the peak's south side above Lyman Lake. Curiously, USGS survey crews swapped this peak's name with Bonanza Peak's on the original 1904 topographic map, and the mix-up stuck.
beta: From a camp at Lyman Lakes, leave the trail and hike cross-country across open meadow, then up talus and scree (Class 2) on the south side of the mountain, with the final push to the summit on looser, steeper Class 2-3 rock. The peak is commonly combined with adjacent Cloudy Peak (about 0.9 mi away) from the same basin camp.

first_pass.evidence: Reports describe a gully then a scramble up the SW ridge to the top; no class number online, record's own rock_grade puts the summit step at Class 3-4 ('3.5')
first_pass.note: Headline Class 2-3 contradicts the record's own Class 3-4 crux

face: East side, direct from the LeConte Glacier
overview: A short, roped alternative to the standard scramble: 2 to 3 pitches of easy/moderate 5th-class climbing rising directly from the LeConte Glacier up Old Guard's east side.
beta: An alternative to the West Side/Southwest scramble: from the LeConte Glacier, climb 2 to 3 pitches of easy/moderate class 5 rock directly up the peak's east side to the summit. It receives far less traffic than the standard snow-couloir-plus-scramble line, and no pitch-by-pitch grades or lengths are on record.

first_pass.evidence: East side: 2-3 pitches of easy/moderate class 5, also described as mid-fifth; no number found

face: North (approached via the notch between Pernod and Chianti)
fa: First ascent 1952 — Don Wilde, Dick McGowan, and Fred Beckey.
overview: Pernod is the highest of the four Wine Spires (Burgundy, Chianti, Chablis, and Pernod) above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey, Dick McGowan, and Don Wilde made the first ascent in September 1952, an aid-heavy climb by today's standards: pitons for both protection and direct aid, a hand-drilled Rawl-drive bolt to protect an insecure section, another bolt to facilitate an 8-foot pendulum around an overhanging, holdless corner, and more bolts placed from a shoulder-stand to reach the summit. The modern
beta: Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.
breakdown: East side to the Pernod–Chianti notch: 4th-5th class

first_pass.evidence: 1952 FA account: ~500 ft of difficult rock to the Pernod-Chianti notch, two hard leads with pitons, a pendulum and a sling near the summit; no modern free grade found online beyond the record's 5.5-5.7.
first_pass.note: Took the top of the record's 5.5-5.7 range; the headline 'Grade III' is a commitment grade, not a difficulty. The first ascent used some aid on the summit section.

face: South-facing hanging glacier above Luna Cirque
overview: The Luna Glacier route is Phantom Peak's original 1940 first-ascent line, named for the small hanging glacier that lies just south of the peak above Luna Cirque (not an officially named glacier, but the moniker stuck). It's a moderate snow-and-easy-rock outing by Pickets standards — Grade II, Easy 5th class — but its remoteness and glacier crux keep it a rarely repeated route.
beta: From Luna Cirque, climb steepening glacier/snow up the hanging glacier below the peak (the technical crux, and reportedly impassable late in the season) to a notch, then transition to rock. Two to three pitches of easy 5th-class slab climbing lead up to the summit ridge; stay off the towers on the south side and climb the final 25-ft summit block directly. Descend by rappelling where possible and downclimbing the route back to the glacier.

first_pass.evidence: Mountain Project: Luna Glacier 'Easy 5th', Steep Snow, M1c; no numeric rock grade found anywhere.
first_pass.note: Brief rule: Easy 5th with no cited number -> 5.0. The record's breakdown '5.2-5.4' is not supported by any source found.
